speechtext:
1.	Has the Minister of Justice received a copy of a radio script of an interview by a Mr. Jack Webster of a Mr. John Banford which was given over station CKLG, North Vancouver, B.C., on Wednesday, March 15, 1961, at 6:10 p.m. and which dealt with Mr. Banford's period of employment at the British Columbia penitentiary during the time that an inmate thereof, a Mr. Johnny Wasly-chen, died while alone and unattended in a dissociation cell the circumstances surrounding which Mr. Banford states he brought to the attention of the Minister of Justice which action Mr. Banford claims brought about his forced resignation?
2.	If so, what action has been taken, or is contemplated, as a result thereof?

speakeroldname: Hon. E. D. Fulton (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: B.C. PENITENTIARY-RESIGNATION FOLLOWING DEATH OF INMATE
speechtext:
The answer to the first question is yes, in that a copy of the script of the broadcast in question was received in the Department of Justice on Monday last.
The answer to the second part is that no action has been taken as a result of this broadcast, nor is any action contemplated because the circumstances are not as implied in the question or in the broadcast.
The facts are that in the course of a visit to the British Columbia penitentiary early in 1960 I decided that certain matters in connection with the administration of the institution required investigation. At that time Mr. Banford placed certain information in the hands of one of my assistants. As a result of the investigation certain administrative changes were made in the institution including a reorganization of the medical department.
I must deny categorically any claim which Mr. Banford makes to the effect that his was a forced resignation. At no time has any action been taken by myself, by the commissioner of penitentiaries or by the warden of the British Columbia penitentiary which was designed to bring about Mr. Banford's resignation or which would have the effect of doing so. The contrary is, in fact, the case. On the occasion,

last September, of a review of Mr. Banford's efficiency rating to determine whether his annual statutory increase in salary should be granted, it was the recommendation of the warden that the increase should be granted. The increase was approved at headquarters and it was granted accordingly.
However, on February 8 this year, many months after the actions referred to earlier were completed, Mr. Banford submitted his resignation in writing to the warden and this was accepted. On February 15 he addressed the following note to the warden:
I am unable to accept that you have been fully informed of the causes of, and circumstances leading to, my resignation. I respectfully ask a hearing on the matter.
On February 17 the warden sent to this officer a memorandum informing him that his resignation had been sent to the commissioner of penitentiaries, and added the following:
If you wish to record any causes or circumstances which led you to the decision to resign I would request that you detail them in full in writing so that they may be forwarded to the commissioner for attachment to your resignation. I shall make arrangements to try and see you next week after your submission is received.
By memorandum dated February 22 Mr. Banford informed the warden as follows:
After careful consideration I have decided that to submit reasons for, and circumstances leading up to, my resignation to the commissioner of penitentiaries would not be the proper course to take in the circumstances.
The facts make it clear that Mr. Banford's resignation was submitted of his own volition and that he himself declined to submit reasons therefor.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
On April 1 we will be entering on a new fiscal year, Mr. Chairman. The main estimates for the new fiscal year have already been tabled. The present resolution and the legislation that it foreshadows seek a vote of supply required to


meet the expenses of government for the months of April and May.
In general, one sixth of all items is requested and with respect to 15 items in particular additional fractions of the items in question are requested, these in all cases relating to programs which do not fit precisely into the month by month succession of the 12 months of the fiscal year. In general, these are programs that require to be expedited or advanced during the earlier part of the fiscal year.
I give the usual undertaking. The passing of the bill to be founded on the resolution will not prejudice the rights and privileges of hon. members to criticize any item in the estimates when it comes up for consideration in the committee of supply. I give the usual undertaking that such rights and privileges will be protected and will not in any way be curtailed or restricted as the result of the passing of this measure.

Mr. Chairman, the request of the government for interim supply gives hon. members of the commons an opportunity to exercise their historic, constitutional right of introducing questions for consideration and if necessary for redress and raising grievances if they so desire before the supply is granted.
The minister has asked us for interim supply reserving all the rights of hon. members for discussion subsequently when the estimates are introduced and supply is requested again. The hon. gentleman has made the request for interim supply in order to meet part of a record level of governmental expenditure which has now reached for the year, I think, a figure approaching $6,300 million. With the supplementaries that have already been brought down and without considering any further ones that may be brought down, this figure, I believe, is over $400 million above that of last year.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No supplementaries have been brought down for 1961-62.
I referred to last year's supplementaries.
It indicates a trend.

The estimates and supplementaries indicate a trend of increasing expenditures reaching record levels including something over $1.5 billion for welfare payments to be made by this free enterprise government.
As a result of this and other factors we have now to consider record deficits resulting not only from increased expenditures but from lower revenues which are themselves due very substantially, I think, to the recession in our economy from which we all hope

it will soon emerge; and there are some encouraging signs of that emergence.
That strong hammer in the anvil chorus of constructive criticism against the government, the Toronto Globe and Mail, in an editorial entitled "Diminishing Returns" on January 30, 1961 had this to say, and these are interesting words from the editor of that paper:
If the Diefenbaker government must operate at a deficit-as it has done ever since attaining power -it is better to have the deficit result from the lower revenue produced by reasonable tax rates than from the lower tax revenue produced (as in December) by excessive tax rates. That way, the economy will have a chance to grow; that way, the reasonable tax rates will eventually produce more than the excessive ones; that way, the Diefenbaker government-if it will curb its appetite for spending-can move toward a balanced budget.
Referring to the estimated expenditures the editorial concluded:
This enormous spending does not boost the economy, but throttles it; does not increase the number of jobs, but reduces them; does not provide "security", but makes every Canadian-employed or unemployed-the less secure. Canada's economy cannot afford this sort of profligacy; the December tax returns show it; Mr. Fleming should see them for what they are-handwriting on the wall.
As I have just said the cessation of expansion in our economy is largely responsible for the situation. I quote from an article by Mr. Ronald Anderson in the Toronto Globe and Mail of January 26, 1961:
Canada's economic growth has slowed almost to a standstill during the past four years. Since 1956 the dollar value of the gross national product has increased by 16 per cent, but in volume terms the gain was less than 6 per cent.
When we consider this situation of very high expenditures which is bound to cause anxiety to anyone who has at heart the welfare of the country and the employment of its citizens, we should remind ourselves that all these expenditures come out of our pockets as taxpayers. All of them are made by us directly through taxes or indirectly, if we try to escape this obligation, by runaway inflation. Nevertheless it is true that, in a time of economic stringency or unemployment, emergency tax adjustments may at times have to be made which would certainly not be justified in more normal and expansive conditions.
It is also true that in a time of emergency and stringency, expenditures may have to be made which would not be justified under normal conditions.
It was not very long ago that this government told the country that the solution for our problems was through huge expenditures for public works. That solution which was a phony one from the beginning in the terms in which it was put has, of course, recently been dropped, so to speak, by none other
Interim Supply
than the Minister of Public Works himself. However, as I have said, in these situations there are times when expenditures which normally would not be justified may have to be made. There are various kinds of expenditures and the government should be very selective when they are made. That selection should be based on the expanding of the economy that the expenditures will create and not on saddling the economy with extra expenditures which will be still there in their effect when the economy has gone through its period of stringency and emergency.
The governor of the Bank of Canada in his very important and interesting report, about which I will have something more to say shortly, has this to say on page 12 with regard to expenditure, and we are being asked this afternoon in this committee to meet at least some of that expenditure:
In particular, investment in human capital can at times do more for growth of output than investment in physical capital. Improved education in general, higher education for a larger proportion of those leaving high school, technological development and training, scientific research, and the development of skills and aptitudes of the widest diversity as required in modern industry, can produce very marked increases in productivity and in total production.
That substantiates my own argument that if we have to make expenditures in this kind of situation they should be expenditures designed to increase productivity. The governor goes on to say:
Such an improvement in human capital can help to develop new forms of industry and rapid expansion in the advanced technologies more effectively than can be achieved merely by straining for more and more physical investment whether provided by foreign investors or otherwise.
In the economic and fiscal measures which the government may have to take to provide for the expenditures which they feel are required, there cannot be satisfactory and constructive results without associating measures in the field of economic and fiscal policy with monetary policy itself, indeed, monetary policy is directly related to high expenditures and to deficits. It will be no surprise to the committee, Mr. Chairman, when I say that we feel that in this field of monetary policy there has been a shocking lack of co-ordination between the government and the Bank of Canada, the bank which is responsible for action in the monetary field, though in our view the government itself must remain responsible ultimately for the policies within which action is taken.
This matter has caused a great deal of discussion in the country and has a direct bearing on today's request for supply. It arose the other day at the Conservative convention. When the Minister of Finance was asked a

Interim Supply
question on the subject he is reported in the Toronto Star as having replied as follows:
... the Bank of Canada was responsible for monetary policy while the government was concerned with fiscal matters. However, since both fields offered an opportunity to deal with economic problems, their policies should be parallel and harmonious.
Of course, Mr. Chairman, the minister is correct in saying that their policies should be parallel and harmonious; and surely it is the responsibility of any government to take steps to ensure, by accepting responsibility for policy, that these policies are parallel and harmonious. Yet the government has refused not only to take the steps that are required but to accept any responsibility for taking those steps. Again, I quote the following from the Globe and Mail of February 23, 1961.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister; Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: You should quote this morning's Globe and Mail.

I read the Globe and Mail every morning. The editorial reads in part as follows:
It is pitiful to see a minister of the crown so clearly contradicting himself for the sake of political expediency.
The editorial is dealing with the question of responsibility for monetary policy.
Yet we can stand the humiliation of a minister. What is not tolerable is that a responsible minister, for the sake of political expediency, should perpetuate and spread, within the country and abroad, dangerous confusion concerning economic policy.
Particularly the Minister of Finance.

Within the country and
abroad, says the Globe and Mail, it is intolerable that a responsible minister, for the sake of political expediency, should perpetuate and spread this dangerous confusion. Surely it is time that parliament looked into this matter to see what can be done to remove these confusions and to ensure, in the words of the minister, that in the field of monetary policy the Bank of Canada and the government should be harmonious and proceeding on parallel courses. That is why we have been asking the government for weeks now to refer this very important report of the Bank of Canada to a committee of the house. Indeed, it is perhaps the most important report by the Bank of Canada that has yet appeared. We asked for this procedure before the report itself appeared and in answer to earlier questions we were told that when the time came shortly for the tabling of the report that would be the time to decide what should be done about it.

After the report was tabled we asked again that it should be submitted to a committee. In fact, I asked the Prime Minister only yesterday to have the report submitted to the banking and commerce committee of the house for purposes which I have already indicated are so important, and the Prime Minister stated in reply that this was a matter for determination by the committee itself. We are asking now that this report should go to this committee or some special committee. If the banking and commerce committee, because it is overburdened with work or for some other reason, does not wish to examine this most important report dealing with this very important matter, then we ask that it should go to a special committee. The report does not deal only with the most important question of monetary policy. There is much in it that goes beyond monetary policy. Therefore if the banking and commerce committee is not in a position to deal with it we ask that it be submitted to a special committee.
Indeed, Mr. Chairman, this is a course which has already been recommended in an impressive way by the Ottawa Journal in an editorial on March 16 from which I can perhaps quote a few words.
It might be said that the governor of the bank should not have thus to explain his mysteries to parliament-*
By appearing before a committee.
-else in the event he appeared to lose the detachment and dignity that should be his. The Journal rejects this.
We on this side reject it too.
We reject it for we are not suggesting he appear before one of the conventional committees such as banking and commerce, where there would be the conventional push and pull, pouncing and defending, clamour and confusion.
Parenthetically may I say that would seem to be a little hard on the banking and commerce committee. If that committee decided to look into this matter we are confident that it would do a good job, but that is a confidence which is not shared by the editor of the Ottawa Journal. The editor goes on to say:
A smaller and well-selected committee, probing rather political, could surely serve here a purpose as useful to Mr. Coyne as to parliament itself. Mr. Coyne has elected to take his case to the country in public speeches. The Journal has commended him for this and for the courage of his assertions. But if he is to step down from the eyrie of his bank to state his views to the people he should also be available to the cross-examination of the people, to the enlightenment of both.
We ask the government to take action which will make possible this examination of the governor's report and of the governor. The Minister of Finance has already indicated, in answer to a question by the hon. member

for Kenora-Rainy River, that he is going to make a report to the house on this matter during the current week.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I did not say a
report.
Perhaps "report" is the wrong word.
An announcement of great significance.

The minister said he would deal with the matter next week, and that is this week. If we are to be informed in due course that a royal commission is to be set up on monetary policy, that will not meet the objectives which we have in mind and which I am attempting to state today. No royal commission, Mr. Chairman, can take away from the members of this committee their right or their duty to examine this matter which is one of immediate and great importance. A royal commission might be used as a device to shelve this whole question for years. We are asking this government for an examination of this matter now on the basis of the report which has been tabled and which, I think I am right in saying, has been considered by a committee of this house in the past.
I hope the minister will be able to reassure us on this point before he asks us to take action in regard to interim supply. I am thinking of an examination of this report not merely because it deals strictly with monetary policy, important though that is. I am thinking of the statements made in this report by the governor of the Bank of Canada which go far beyond monetary policy and which enter the field of fiscal and economic policy. These statements indicate that the governor has some ideas or some proposals which might help this country out of some of its economic difficulties. It is because of the importance of those statements by this important man that I venture, before I sit down, to read from this report, and to substantiate my statement that it goes far beyond the strict operation of monetary policy. I am not criticizing the governor for doing this because it has been done in past reports.
Mr. Coyne has this to say as recorded at the bottom of page 16 of this report:
Large-scale unemployment is an indication of failure on the part of all of us collectively to make the most effective use of the resources of modern technology and social organization. When the economy as a whole operates at less than full capacity-
That is the situation now with 726,000 people out of work.
-we are not producing the maximum possible supply of goods and services for use today, either for consumption or for increasing our capacity to provide a higher rate of production and a higher
Interim Supply
standard of living tomorrow. The nation as a whole suffers real economic loss, and it is avoidable economic loss, in addition to the personal loss and frustration of those particular persons who are seeking work and unable to find it. It seems to me only common sense, when considering the economic, social and personal problems of unemployment, that no price is too great for the community as a whole to pay in order to achieve full production and reduce unemployment to the lowest possible level.
That is a very important, straightforward statement from a man who is in a very responsible position and who has great authority and responsibility in the field of monetary policy. Surely it would be proper to examine the governor and the officials of the bank on statements of that kind. I should like Mr. Coyne to elaborate and perhaps be a little more definite about what can be done to realize the objectives which he has set out in this paragraph and which he says can be realized if the community is willing to do so.
Then the report goes on in this way:
A central bank must be opposed to inflationary methods which involve excessive monetary expansion.
There can be no quarrel with that statement.
But the adoption of any policy or any combination of policies directed towards establishing and maintaining full employment, and maintaining a high rate of steadily continuing economic growth without inflation, is not in any way prevented or limited by the central bank or by a sound money policy.
Presumably what the governor of the Bank of Canada means by that is that if there is a sound monetary policy-he asserts that the monetary policy followed by the bank has been sound-then within that policy and without inflation the government can take steps in the fiscal and economic fields to bring about and maintain a high level of employment. As Mr. Coyne puts it:
There is no financial obstacle to the carrying out in a non-inflationary way of any program which is physically possible, if the community is willing to make the appropriate arrangements and put into effect whatever changes in the use of physical resources and changes in the distribution of real incomes may be involved in such programs.
Something else is required, Mr. Chairman, in addition to the will of the community and that is sound, bold and strong leadership on the part of the government of the day. This is what we are requesting. Every member of the House of Commons has his own responsibility to assist in this regard. Surely it would be desirable, if it is practicable, to have this report and the matters contained in it submitted to a committee of this House of Commons.
I should like to give one more quotation from Mr. Coyne, following what I have just read. He says:

Interim Supply
These are the real factors involved, which cannot be avoided, whatever method be favoured to deal with them.
He is talking about the will of the community to take action. I have added the requirement of sound, bold and strong leadership on the part of the government. He says:
Inflation itself is one method of inducing changes and adjustments in the use of physical resources and in the distribution of real incomes-but there must be more equitable and efficient ways, better ways of sharing the real costs and ultimate benefits of full employment policy and other constructive economic and social policies.
These are impressive words in an impressive and, in some respects perhaps, controversial report. Because it is so impressive and because in some respects it is controversial this report should be examined by a committee of this house. This matter should not be referred to any royal commission as a device for avoiding a parliamentary examination. Therefore, before supply is granted, we ask the minister, whether or not he can give us some reassurance that this procedure will be followed.

The country faces at the moment a very grave unemployment situation which, as has been demonstrated in the figures made available today, is steadily worsening. Monetary policy has a very important effect on the economy, the whole problem of unemployment, surplus agricultural commodities and other important economic questions. When the Minister of Finance was in opposition he complained about high interest rates, and about the tight money policy the former government was following. He complained that they were not following a policy of lower interest rates and an expanded money supply. Now that the minister is in office, he seems to be determined to do exactly the opposite of what he recommended when he was in opposition and to adopt policies which are the opposite of those he put forward at that time.
The country faces a grave unemployment situation. The government has failed to deal with it. The statistics cannot be pooh-poohed or laughed off, even if hon. gentlemen opposite would like to do so. These figures not only show 719,000 unemployed in the week ended February 18 but show that in certain parts of Canada this matter of unemployment is extremely serious. They show that 18 per cent of the labour force is unemployed in the Atlantic region. This government has not put forward any program to deal with the problems in that region. When questions regarding coal policy are raised the government holds a conference but does not decide upon any policy. There is almost one person in five unemployed in the maritimes.

The figures show that 14.5 per cent of the labour force is unemployed in Quebec. This means that one person in seven suffers all the miseries of hardship, physical and mental, which flow from such a situation. Still the government does not act. Apparently the government is not concerned about this unemployment because it refuses to take steps to find a solution to the problem.
Let us consider these figures in regard to the prairie region where we find a better situation than that in the rest of Canada but still 7.1 per cent of the labour force is unemployed, or one person in 14.
The unemployment situation in the Pacific region is exceedingly bad, with 13.9 per cent of the labour force unemployed, or approximately one person in seven.
In the province of Ontario these figures show that 8.6 per cent of the labour force is unemployed. This a serious situation. It is not quite as bad as the national average, but still it is severe. This indicates that one person in 12 is unemployed. Although the province of Ontario is relatively better off in regard to unemployment than are most of the other provinces, nevertheless, in the great city of Toronto public welfare officers have made the statement that there is hunger in the city, that people are suffering from the lack of food. In spite of this situation the government fails to take any action with regard to monetary and other policies.
The governor of the Bank of Canada has been criticized very severely in recent days. The Minister of Finance takes a rather strange attitude towards this criticism. He states that the Bank of Canada is entirely separate from the government. The Minister of Finance states that he is not responsible for anything the Bank of Canada does, or for any statement made by the governor of the Bank of Canada. According to the Minister of Finance the Bank of Canada and the governor are laws unto themselves. Although this seems to be an alibi that the minister is putting forward, it would seem to me that the government must agree with the policies that are followed by the Bank of Canada or the government would change those policies. Surely in our democracy we have not yet arrived at the point where the government can say that all of these things are the responsibility of the Bank of Canada, that the government has abdicated its responsibility and that the Bank of Canada is running the country.
I believe the record will show that I made this suggestion first during this session, but in any event the opposition members of both parties have asked time after time that this whole question of monetary policy be referred

to the banking and commerce committee. The minister has taken a non-committal attitude in this regard. He has not said that this will not be done or that he opposed it, but has just not taken any step to see that it is done. When I asked him a question in this regard on December 8 he replied that the annual report of the Bank of Canada had not been received but that when it was received the house could take action if it wished to do so. I suggest that now is the time for the government to send that annual report to the banking and commerce committee where a full inquiry can be made into central bank policies and into depressed economic conditions which exist throughout the country. I would suggest that it is perhaps of greater importance that an inquiry be made into the financial policies which are now being followed by the government, and in order to regularize such a procedure I would suggest that this parliament should refer not only the Bank of Canada report to that committee but also the estimates of the Department of Finance. The Minister of Finance should also be available to that committee in order to answer questions. Let us turn the spotlight of public opinion on this colossal failure of the government to deal with the economic crisis currently facing the Canadian nation.
Instead of dealing with this unemployment problem the government seems determined to adopt measures that will make a solution more difficult. High interest rates have made borrowings by provincial governments very difficult. High interest rates have rendered the whole question of municipal finances almost unbearable. Nevertheless the minister is apparently content with the very high interest rates being paid in this country today. They may be all right from the minister's point of view because the government has almost unlimited powers of taxation, but they are certainly not all right from the point of view of provincial governments, many of which have been forced into deficit budget positions, a situation which has placed unbearable burdens on the municipalities in this country. I suggest that now is the time for the government to end this high interest rate policy and to reduce the interest rate as a start on a program that will provide full employment.
It would be interesting to have the governor of the Bank of Canada before the banking and commerce committee because he has said that he knows how to solve the unemployment problem without any inflation taking place. This is the man with the greatest responsibility in regard to monetary policy in Canada and he says in his annual report
Interim Supply
that we in Canada can have full employment without inflation. Apparently this government is not prepared to have his programs spelled out by having Mr. Coyne appear before the banking and commerce committee.
If the Minister of Finance is not interested in the question of recession and widespread unemployment personally, he should be interested from a political standpoint. Not only is the country suffering generally from unemployment. I would suggest there is every indication that the Tory party is suffering through its failure to solve the problem.
The governor of the Bank of Canada has said in his report that there is no financial obstacle to the carrying out in a non-inflationary way of any program which is physically possible, if the community is willing to make the appropriate arrangements and to put into effect whatever changes in the use of physical resources and changes in the distribution of real incomes may be involved in such programs. The governor of the Bank of Canada says further that we can have full production and full employment, and can do all of these things in a non-inflationary way. The Minister of Finance on the other hand apparently does not want to hear about this, and does not want to listen to Mr. Coyne give details of this program. He refuses to have this annual report considered by the banking and commerce committee, but I would suggest that is the way in which to deal with this subject.
I would suggest that the way to deal with the problem of unemployment in Canada today is quite clear.
The government has to undertake policies of the same kind as those that were undertaken by a Liberal administration during the war. This problem has to be attacked by an expansion in the money supply, by an increase in the purchasing power in the pockets of the people of this country and by calling on the people of this nation to invest their own money in the productive resources of our own country and not to depend on United States money. This policy should be followed by one of price regulations when necessary in order to prevent an increase in the general price level.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, would the hon. member permit a question? He is of course familiar with the debates we used to have years ago on this subject, and he understands that it was pointed out by those who were administering price controls that they could not enforce them without wage controls. Do I understand that the hon. member is advocating wage controls as well?

I know that the minister thinks this is a really tough question, but I do not

Interim Supply
think so. I think wage control flows from price control. You do not have to set a rigid control on wages in order to have the level of wages influenced and largely controlled by the price level. Show me any depressed industry in Canada today and I will show you an industry where wages are low.
There is no arbitrary control of the wage level in the coal industry, but wages are low. There is an arbitrary control at the moment although there have been attempts in the past-and we may get a dose of it soon-to freeze the wages of the railway workers, but they are very much controlled because in recent years this industry has not been one of much profit.
Therefore in answer to the question of the Minister of Finance I would reply that we in this party say there should be a control of prices in the key industries in this country. If you regulate prices, this control in itself has a very definite influence on wages. I may say to the minister that some of the people most strongly in support of price regulations are the workers and their organizations who would be affected, along with other Canadians, by any such policy being followed.
However, I think we have an issue at the moment, as the Prime Minister has so aptly put it, between free enterprise and socialism. The government is so married to the free enterprise system, and it so loves the profits of the big corporations and the high interest rates paid to the finance institutions of this country that it refuses to take the steps necessary to solve the unemployment crisis because this might mean some control of the economy.
We know that the Liberal party is not in favour of controls. They have said all along that they would not go for price regulations. They are also a free enterprise party.
You do not know what you are talking about.
They are strong in condemnation but they are short on programs and alternative procedures.
Keep the debate on an objective plane.
Coming from the hon. member for Essex East, this is rather difficult to take, because I think the hon. member is probably the least objective member of the house.
But he is not a socialist.

However, he will have an opportunity in a few moments, no doubt, to deal with this matter. The hon. member for Essex East has so much difficulty with his

own statements that he should not worry about the content of statements of other hon. members.
We shall undoubtedly hear the policy of the Liberal party when the hon. member for Essex East makes his contribution, and I look forward to it very much. However, I very much doubt that the Liberal party will come out in favour of price regulations along with a massive attack on unemployment. They say they can make a few short cuts and a few tiny modifications that will allow big business to run the country in the future as it does today. But they say they are going to solve the problem of unemployment, where the Conservatives have failed.
The Liberal party has a long record in this country, and in past years there has been very high unemployment under a Liberal government.

That is not the
fact.

I suggest that the minister should consider the plea that has been made to him this afternoon to have the annual report of the Bank of Canada referred to the banking and commerce committee. I would ask him to also consider referring the estimates of the Department of Finance to this committee. Let us have a full public inquiry. Let us find out how Mr. Coyne and other experts can deal with the very difficult recession in which this country now finds itself.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in introducing his remarks earlier this afternoon the Leader of the Opposition spoke of the historic and constitutional right which members of parliament have on an occasion such as this. That right is to raise grievances or deal with matters concerning which the Minister of Finance is now seeking interim supply.
There is one such matter with which I should like to deal, and I should like to do so in an objective and constructive manner. It concerns a subject matter which has been under discussion here on a number of occasions, and it concerns a very important industry which exists in several parts of Canada but more particularly in the provinces of Quebec and Ontario. I refer, of course, to the position of the textile industry.
During the course of the brief remarks which I intend to make I should like to put forward to the minister and the government certain suggestions which I believe are of a constructive nature. I would ask the minister and the government to give consideration to these suggestions.
It has been stated repeatedly in this house and outside that Quebec's big, important textile industry is struggling hard to "hang on".

This statement is contained in an article by Eric Richter in the Financial Post of February 4. The following is stated therein:
For most of the province's 370-odd mills and establishments, 1960 results were disappointing, even when measured against the "lean" years the textile industry has had in the past decade.
As the house knows, evidence was given before the manpower committee of the other place by the president of the primary textiles institute who stated that imported textiles cost 35,000 jobs in the Canadian textile industry last year and that the situation is going to get worse unless something is done.
In this morning's Globe and Mail there appears an article which I am sure the Minister of Finance, the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Minister of National Revenue have seen. The article is entitled:
Looking into business
The quiet Canadians were not exactly wasting their time.
I shall read but one paragraph. It is bylined "Hong Kong, March 21" and reads:
Finance Minister Donald Fleming's special Hong Kong mission aimed at persuading local textile manufacturers to limit their exports to Canada was doomed to failure even before it started. Yet It shouldn't be thought that the mission was a waste of time. Mr. Fleming sent to Hong Kong the director-general of the international and economic affairs branch, S. S. Reisman, and two colleagues. Canada's trade commissioners in Hong Kong, C. M. Forsyth-Smith and C. J. Small also assisted the three Ottawa delegates in their talks with local exporters, textile producers and government officials.
Although the Canadians did not convince Hong Kong's textile men that they should impose voluntary restraints, both sides at least came to grips with a problem that is causing increasing concern in Canada's textile industry. Despite a huge markup at the Canadian end, Hong Kong shirts, for example, often sell at half or two thirds of the price of Canadian-made shirts.
There is no doubt that the situation is a very serious one. That fact has been emphasized by the recent closing of two mills at Grand'Mere-the Grand'Mere Knitting Company mill and the Grand'Mere Handcraft Company mill-as revealed in an article published in La Presse on March 15 entitled "Decision Brutale a Grand'Mere". The two mills closed down and put out of work no less than 300 employees who are now looking for other employment. Of course, the committee knows *-and I need not repeat it-that mills in the vicinity of Hamilton, three mills in the community of Cornwall and mills elsewhere have closed down. My purpose in rising this afternoon is not to stress that aspect of the situation but rather to offer the minister some ideas of a constructive nature. I do not pose as an expert; indeed, I am far from being an expert on this very important question but there are others who are experts. I have been in consultation with someone who is an expert in this field. I have spent some time
Interim Supply
with him, and any credit that there may be for the suggestions I am about to put on record must go to this individual and not to me.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I would rather not do so, but I should be happy to give the hon. parliamentary secretary the pamphlets which I have in mind and which have been written by him. This individual has written three pamphlets on this important subject. The first is entitled: "What the Canadian Textile Industry can Produce which it is not now Producing". The second is called: "How the Canadian Textile Industry can Compete with Imports". The third is entitled: "How the Canadian Textile Industry can Export". These are three pamphlets which I shall be glad at any time to show to the Minister of Finance, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, the Minister of National Revenue or their parliamentary secretaries for them to consider. As I said earlier, any credit for the suggestions contained in them should go to this individual and to nobody else, if they are found to be sound.
I have attempted to summarize as briefly as possible the main contents of these pamphlets. It is, of course, impossible in the 15 or 20 minutes at my disposal to give a complete summary of what is contained in these briefs, but I should like to put on record the main suggestions which are contained therein because I believe they are worthy of careful consideration.
The primary textile industry in Canada ranks second among the manufacturing industries of this country. No one in this committee, I am sure, will dispute the fact that this industry has fallen on very hard times in recent years. Even though some of the new textile companies may be efficient, there is an evident need for more co-ordination of effort on the part of all the component parts of the textile industry. For example, there is a need for better marketing techniques, more imaginative processing, better and greatly increased research methods, more investigation of new projects and a firmer will to export. All of these ideas need to permeate the Canadian textile industry.
Because the industry is so important to the Canadian economy, one might have thought that the Department of Trade and Commerce would already have taken steps to bring about some of this co-ordination. However, this appears not to be the case. I make this statement knowing full well that the Minister of Trade and Commerce called a conference of all the trade commissioners here in Canada. Whether or not there were

Interim Supply
present experts or representatives of the textile industry I am unable to say. However, I do not believe there was any decision on the part of those who were convened in the office of the minister on that occasion to seek to encourage the export of textile goods from this country. It may be that the new productivity council which was established recently by the government will provide an agency allowing the necessary co-ordination to be done. However, from the composition and the limited terms of reference of the productivity council it does not appear likely that this would be so.
I should like now to make a specific suggestion that the government should take the lead in bringing together various members of the textile industry and assisting them in the formation of a textile co-ordinating council. That is one of the many suggestions recommended in these three briefs. Some of the functions of this council would be as follows:
(a)	The investigation of better or cheaper sources of raw materials and the study of their applications.
(b)	Preparation of a detailed study of all existing textile processes from preparatory operations through blending, weaving, knitting, felting, dyeing, and finishing with a view to improving the quality and versatility of the end products.
(c)	Improvement of merchandising, starting with accurate labelling and proceeding through consumer education.
(d)	Continuous research in the field of development of new fibres; detailed studies of their properties and limitations.
(e)	Encouraging industry to develop new techniques necessary to fully utilize newly developed synthetic fibres.
(f)	Analysis of consumer demands in development of products which are custom-built to meet these demands.
(g)	Collection and indexing of technical and statistical data on all phases of the textile industry in all parts of the world.
(h)	Perhaps the council could consider the organization and maintenance of a Canadian textile museum containing representative samples of all available textile products.
(j) The council could act as technical adviser to the government and legislation pertaining to the textile industry. The council should develop very close relationship with the Department of Trade and Commerce.
The need, therefore, for this co-ordinating body seems to be painfully evident. The fact that the industry has difficulty in competing with imports indicates that development work on new products is far behind, and for that reason I strongly urge the government to give serious consideration to the formation of a textile co-ordinating council. It seems to

me this might be done either separately or as a subcommittee of the productivity council, although because of the importance of the industry it would perhaps be far better if it were established separately and apart from the productivity council.
There are in addition two areas in which this co-ordinating council could be of great assistance to the textile industry and I should like to further elaborate on this matter. The first is the encouragement of the industry to do research into new products and to use the resources of Canada in manufacturing these new products. One illustration of the type of research I envisage is this. It stands to reason that we should use the great amount of wood pulp that we possess in this country. This could be done if we were to manufacture viscose. If we were to blend 20 per cent viscose with 80 per cent cotton this would mean better products and more use of Canadian resources. The production of the necessary amount of viscose would provide for thousands of Canadian workers and employment resulting from the use of our natural resources in imaginative processes. This ought to be, surely, our first aim.
I have before me a note indicating that we use in Canada about 300,000 bales of cotton a year. I am informed that if we were to mix 80 per cent of that baled cotton with 20 per cent viscose this would mean that an industry such as Courtauld's (Canada) Limited, for instance, would have to produce about 30 million pounds more viscose. It would mean thousands more jobs in substituting the viscose for the baled cotton.
I am also informed that there may be other areas in Canada where viscose might be produced. If after a careful study by the textile council as to whether or not this can be done-and I am informed from authoritative sources that it can be done- then here is a method by which not only can competition be better met but, more particularly, additional jobs can be obtained.
It has also been pointed out to me that in the opening of the vast regions of our north country we are faced with the problem of building roads on muskeg. We ought to investigate woven and non-woven fabrics which could be instrumental in overcoming the peculiar difficulties connected with this problem in the north country. In that area there are also a number of other needs to which the textile industry could contribute a solution. For example the present tents could be improved with the thermo insulation built into the fibre. Arctic clothing will have to have the insulation built into the fibre and into the woven, non-woven or

knitted fabric. There are many other imaginative ways in which the textile industry could develop products for the north.
The number of new products which could be utilized staggers the imagination. Let me give the committee a few illustrations. As the committee knows, there is a great need for light-weight strong filaments, fibres, yarns, threads and rope. There is also no chenille to speak of produced in Canada. There is a need for various types of chenille which can be produced with blends of cotton, wool or silk. Such a product has innumerable applications never before produced in Canada such as knitted chenille outer wear, head squares, shawls, sport shawls, travelling plaids, chenille bathing and beach wear.
In the field of woollens and worsteds, by blending with high priced fibres like vicuna, camel hair, kemp and mohair products of an exceptionally high quality can be produced. New products like woollen chenille and woollen and silk-blended chenille which have innumerable uses for fine outer wear are possible.
As the committee knows, in the province of Quebec there is a special situation. There are in that province skilled workers who for many years have been directing their attention to a large number of articles that have a particular attraction in the province. There are, for example, wonderful local products the market for which could be greatly enlarged. I refer to such things as blankets, hooked rugs, shawls, felt slippers and felt skirts. None of these products is now being merchandised nearly enough.
Another product is the very popular Quebec blanket. This is a typical Quebec small industry. Some of these blankets have wonderful designs and there is a fantastic potential market for them with the proper merchandising. Long range policies for these articles in the province of Quebec should be given consideration and in order to give them the sales interest which they should have, we must be ahead of everyone else. We must have good research and consideration must be given to creating attractive designs and selling these goods in quantity in other countries. How is it, for instance, that articles made in Switzerland such as woollen sweaters and blankets are being sold here sometimes in greater numbers than are our own products simply because of the design?
If it were possible, as these pamphlets indicate, to create a newer design which would bring out, for instance, the Quebec folklore and which would lay emphasis on the art of the province of Quebec, it would then be
Interim Supply
quite possible to sell an attractive article which would compete here and in other countries.
In the field of plied fabrics there are again many products which should be investigated including items which have never been produced in Canada such as portable kayaks and other portable boats, diving suits and improved anti-gravity suits. These items immediately come to mind.
The second point I wish to elaborate slightly is the fact that there are great potential export markets for these typical Canadian products. Here I am willing to pay tribute to the Department of Trade and Commerce. It is encouraging to see that department is livening up in the area of increased Canadian exports. The textile industry badly needs similar stimulus for export. It urgently requires all types of information relating to exports such as foreign market conditions, shipping requirements, foreign prices and the like.
If the government would take the initiative in setting up this textile co-ordinating council which has been recommended, most of the information needed to stimulate export could be made readily available to the textile industry. By integrating the components of the textile industry in this country, the textile co-ordinating council could make a great contribution to the vitality of this major Canadian industry and could provide jobs for thousands of Canadian workers.
All I ask of the government and of the Minister of Finance and his colleagues who I am sure are interested in this industry, is that consideration be given to the suggestions I have made and to the contents of these three pamphlets to which I have referred. I urge them to consider the suggestions of an expert in this field who has had a great deal to do with matters such as this and who has already been in communication with a large number of textile industries in the central part of Canada. If that consideration is given I would hope the government will see fit, having regard to all the circumstances, to establish a textile council which would coordinate all activities of that industry.

Mr. Chairman, the speech made this afternoon by the Leader of the Opposition, it seems to me, touches the most important issue before parliament at this time, because the implications of the report presented by the governor of the Bank of Canada touch the heart of the major problem that confronts us in Canada. I join in the remarks he has made today and support them because of the apparent reluctance of the Minister of Finance to deal with them. Certainly this reluctance has been displayed not only during this debate but whenever the question has been raised.
The question takes on added importance in the light of the disclosure yesterday and the formal release this morning of the figures as to the present unemployment situation. These figures show that our labour force is down
33.000	compared with the previous reported period. It is the first decrease, by the way, since 1958. They show employment down
59.000	compared with the previous reported period. It also indicates that it is up only
25.000	over the figure of a year ago. In addition, of course, there is the dismal news that the present unemployment figure in our country on the basis of the lowest accepted standard, that of the dominion bureau of statistics, is 719,000.
This is a record figure, and it would seem to me that when the governor of the Bank of Canada deals with the capacity of this nation to provide full employment the government, and in particular the Minister of Finance, will be remiss if the statement made so ably today by the Leader of the Opposition is not answered. The unemployment statistics establish also that they are higher by 121,000 than they were a year ago, for the same period, and that they represent an increase of 26,000 over the previous month.
I am happy to note that the increase is not as great as one had been led to believe from the indices. The satisfaction one derives from the present figure is certainly less than one might have hoped. I would hope it is an indication that forces of growth are present that might lead to an end of the recession but from what we now know there is no reason to believe that this necessarily will be accompanied by a reduction on a proportionate basis of unemployment itself.
It seems to me that this is an issue to which the Minister of Finance cannot fail to address himself. He can take the position that he does not propose to answer the observations made by the Leader of the Opposition. He can take the position that the

report of the governor of the Bank of Canada is a matter only for parliament. He can take the position that he refuses to say whether or not he is prepared to support the move to have the governor of the Bank of Canada appear before the banking and commerce or any other committee, designed for that purpose by this house. He can take all of these positions. He can sit mute and refuse to make any acknowledgement whatsoever; but if that is the position that he will ultimately take, all I would say, is that he will warrant the criticisms made a few weeks ago by the Toronto Globe and Mail with regard to what he had to say on a matter not unrelated to this question.
If the observations made by the governor of the Bank of Canada do not stand in the position of opposing the policies of the government, they at least stand in the position that there are no known declarations made by any of the ministers of the government, more particularly the Minister of Finance, that support the contentions made by the governor of the Bank of Canada. The government, when it is confronted with the problem of unemployment, now says that the responsibility lies on labour and on management. That is not what the governor of the Bank of Canada says. This is not the only inconsistency between the position taken by the government and that taken by the governor of the Bank of Canada, as the Leader of the Opposition indicated in a number of references he made to the recent report of the governor of the bank. I add these further observations of the governor of the Bank of Canada. As found on page 23 of his report to parliament he has this to say at the bottom of the page:
If I may quote from a recent speech by the governor of the Bank of England, "... A theme which I have myself argued for many years past is that monetary policy cannot cure all ills, and that it is a great mistake to expect it to carry loads which should be carried in other fields of government policy."
That statement is approved by the governor of the Bank of Canada and he then goes on to say:
Lord Cobbold was speaking in this context about the problems of restraining the excesses of a boom, but his theme applies with even greater force to the problems of overcoming recession and promoting a satisfactory rate of sustained economic growth.
Does the Minister of Finance agree with that statement? On page 14 of his report the governor says:
At a time of relatively high unemployment in Canada, it is difficult to avoid the conclusion that the continuing very large deficit in the balance of payments is not only disadvantageous in itself but is indicative of an excessive capital inflow as well as structural weaknesses in the Canadian economy which result in excessive aggregate spending on goods and services provided from abroad

to the detriment of the production of goods and services of a similar character in Canada.
That was your argument too.

I refer now to pages 15 and 16, and I invite the vigilant member for Edmonton West to pay attention to these words. The governor has this to say:
Analysis of our situation seems to me to indicate that the approach to higher employment and output-
I would hope that the Minister of Finance would find it desirable to listen to what is being said.
-should be through measures designed to reduce the large deficit in our current account balance of payments, and through increases in spending of a selective character likely to increase production in Canada, rather than through measures designed to raise the level of total spending by Canadians.
I call the minister's attention to these words.
I am sure that there are many more possible ways of setting up incentives directed towards these goals than is generally realized. One would hope for the most imaginative and thorough canvass of the possibilities and widespread discussion by those who are interested.
I would assume that among those who are interested would be the Minister of Finance and the government of Canada. The governor concludes that paragraph by saying:
Ultimate decisions must rest with the appropriate governmental authorities in accordance with their best assessment of what the national interest and welfare requires.
That statement, the other statements I have quoted and those put on the record by the Leader of the Opposition indicate that the governor of the Bank of Canada does not, and properly so, take responsibility for anything other than monetary policy. He says the monetary policy by itself cannot provide full employment. He then goes on to establish that he, as governor of the Bank of Canada, believes there are within this nation capacities and instruments by which we can achieve full employment. We are asking for the opportunity to ascertain from the governor of the Bank of Canada the details of his remedies. Once we have ascertained what those details are, we want to find out whether or not the government of Canada agrees with them. In that event, we want to find out why the government of Canada has not adopted the proposals made by the governor of the Bank of Canada. We should like to interrogate the governor in order to ascertain whether or not the government has, in fact, sought to make an appreciation of the value of the recommendations made by the governor.

The governor of the Bank of Canada is an important official under our system of government. However, he is not a sovereignty, in himself, as the Minister of Finance suggested some time ago when he divorced the government of any responsibility whatsoever for the conduct and formulation of monetary policy. But the governor of the Bank of Canada has been given by parliament important powers with regard to monetary policy that admittedly he primarily exercises. This does not mean, of course, that the government has no responsibility in the field of monetary policy. The governor has not been talking about monetary policy. In the main he has been talking from one end of Canada to the other about matters which agitate us in this house and which have to do with our capacity as a free enterprise nation to bring about full employment. If the Bank of Canada is responsible to parliament, it is the duty of this government to see to it that we as individual members of parliament are given an opportunity, through a parliamentary committee or otherwise, to obtain the answers to the questions I have outlined, which are among those that we would want to put to the governor of the Bank of Canada.
I join with the Leader of the Opposition in the stand he has taken today, as I did yesterday, for two reasons. First of all, when we are talking about unemployment in this house we are generally made to confront the Minister of Labour. I have always taken the position that the Minister of Labour-and I do not speak of him in a personal way-is not competent to deal exclusively with the question of unemployment, nor is his department capable of doing so by the nature of its organization. Unemployment is a matter that primarily rests on the doorstep of the Department of Finance, in association with certain other departments of government including the Department of Labour. The second reason is that we are entitled to know, before the committee disposes of the request for interim supply, whether or not the government proposes to by-pass parliament and appoint a royal commission, as was done two years ago in the United Kingdom.
There was justification for the appointment of a royal commission in Great Britain two years ago. The terms of reference given to Lord Radcliffe were altogether different from the terms of reference that arise out of any situation in this country at this time. If a royal commission were designated by the government of Canada to deal with monetary policy, we would be precluded in practice from taking any steps to examine the governor of the Bank of Canada with regard to monetary policy, assuming that the terms of reference of the commission were

This is an important matter. This is a matter that goes right to the fundamental issue facing us at the moment. The governor of the Bank of Canada says it is possible to have full employment with varying levels of capital investment and savings, as the history of many countries will show. He made that statement on January 17 when speaking to the annual conference of the business paper editors association in Ottawa. The following day, January 18, the Toronto Globe and Mail reported the governor of the bank in these terms:
"I venture the proposition that it is not healthy and will not be fruitful or successful for a country such as Canada to pursue any other course than to stand on its own feet, finance its own development out of its own savings, and refrain from trying to achieve a rate of economic growth in excess of what its own best efforts can support," he said.
Is that the policy of the government of Canada? We are entitled to know that. We are entitled to know whether or not the Minister of Finance and the governor are in disagreement on this fundamental question. Does the Minister of Finance agree with the

statement of the governor of the Bank of Canada as reported on February 4, 1961, when he said:
It seems to me only common sense . . . that no price is too great for the community as a whole to pay in order to achieve full production and reduce unemployment to the lowest possible level-[DOT]
Does the government agree with that statement? Does the government agree with that recommendation made by the governor of the Bank of Canada to reduce unemployment to its lowest possible level?
Does the government agree with the speech made by the governor of the Bank of Canada in St. John's, Newfoundland, on January 31, 1951, when he said the nation as a whole suffers real economic loss, and it is an avoidable economic loss, in addition to the personal loss and frustration of those particular persons who are seeking work and unable to find it? Does the government agree with that statement? When the governor of the Bank of Canada says this, he must have some reason for doing so. We want to know what his reason is.

in Canada, and that is the people represented by constituted authority, the government of the day. There can be no other authority. The Minister of Finance or the government cannot allow a public official, no matter who that official may be, to parade from one end of this country to another enunciating publicly economic doctrines which he believes should form government policy. It is wrong to allow this to go on without intervention by the government, or any discipline being imposed. The government must affirm that the governor of the bank cannot go on in that manner, and stay within his present assignment if these views are persisted in and publicly declared. For the minister or the government to take any other course is, on the part of this government, an abdication of its responsibilities. This is making the government look silly and is putting it in a subservient position.
If the governor of the Bank of Canada is entitled to express views that are contrary to those expressed by the government of Canada why then are the military staff, the air chief, and the naval chief not allowed to express opinions in public or before Canadian clubs, boards of trade or universities? That of course would be a most unfortunate permission to extend to any military officer and would be a violation of our concept of government. That is exactly what is being done at the present time in an equally important field-the economic field-by the governor of the Bank of Canada. Not one word has been said by this government, to the knowledge of the Canadian people or this parliament, as to whether the government has expressed its view with respect to the propriety of this course. The governor of the Bank of Canada is a very able man and has been well trained for the high post he occupies. He must know the extent of his authority. He must know that his authority is limited to monetary policy. If he persists, as he does, in making these declarations on such a wide economic front, he must be doing it for a purpose. I suggest that purpose is clear. He is concerned about the results of government policy and particularly the policy of the Department of Finance and the consequences of those policies. He must feel that he is serving his country best by making these declarations which are tantamount to warnings to the Canadian people. What other conclusion can one come to?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If that is what the governor is seeking to do, does the hon. member approve of such a course of action?

I certainly do not approve. I am stating that I do not believe

Interim Supply
that under our system of government it is right or proper for a government official, in areas of authority not specifically extended to him by parliament, to take in public a position that puts him in disagreement with the government of the day. That is the position I take. What I have just been saying is that if the governor takes that position, he must be doing it because he feels that, with his knowledge as governor of the Bank of Canada, he owes it to the country to speak in this way and thereby to warn the people about the consequences of present government policy. That can be the only conclusion one can come to when these things are said by a man so reasonable and so well equipped for his job as is the governor of the Bank of Canada.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. I must advise the hon. member that his time has expired.

Mr. Chairman, not being of the same political complexion as one might assume the governor of the Bank of Canada to be, I cannot be so laudatory of him as was the hon. member for Essex East. However, we do know that ever since this government took office there has been a growing conflict between the governor of the Bank of Canada, the Minister of Finance and government policy generally. There has been a growing desire on the part of the government to abdicate their responsibility in the fiscal and monetary field whenever they deem it expedient to do so.
We can recall those short days when we had a minority government before the election of 1958. During that period of time the Minister of Finance, who was not then the minister, and some of his colleagues campaigned on the basis of high interest rates, how they would fix the economy, how parliament would again have sole jurisdiction, and things of that nature. Hardly had the ink dried on these comments and the election been finished when the Minister of Justice, who was then minister of citizenship and immigration or the acting minister, came to British Columbia and attended a series of meetings.
One of these meetings was held on the campus of the University of British Columbia. The minister renounced all responsibility in the monetary field on the part of his government and himself. He said that everything that had been going wrong was really the fault of the Bank of Canada and that the government itself had no responsibility. Perhaps what he was saying indirectly was that the government really had no interest in tackling this major question of monetary policy and its effect upon and relationship

to the economy. The Minister of Finance on various occasions has been engaged in making similar comments.
As I mentioned, Mr. Chairman, one of the key-note cries of the Tories before the 1957 election-I do not think we need dwell on them too long-concerned the question of tight money and how with a tight money policy the Liberals had dragged the economy into a recession or a rolling readjustment, or whatever phrase was used. It was said that all we had to do to solve all these problems was to elect the hon. member for Eglin-ton and his friends who would then become the government and would straighten it all out. But we have seen nothing straightened out. In reality the position has worsened, and it worsens as each day passes. To confirm this statement we have only to witness the figures Which were released prematurely yesterday but which officially came to the attention of hon. members this morning.
At this time it appears that the government does not want to do anything about this situation. The Minister of Finance knows full well that the higher interest rates which he himself imposed foisted upon the Canadian taxpayers an extra burden to the tune of millions and millions of dollars and in reality constitute a drain on the purchasing power of the people of this nation.
I do not understand how on the one hand the minister can endorse this method of draining off the taxpayer's dollar while on the other hand his colleagues say, "Go out and spend yourself into prosperity". How this government can reconcile those two approaches is beyond my understanding. If ever schizophrenia existed in government, it exists here. We all know that this government spent so many years in opposition that it really has not much of a clue on how to conduct the affairs of state. It has so mismanaged the affairs that come under its jurisdiction, especially in the monetary field, that we have existing the condition that was announced today in so far as the number of unemployed is concerned.
Perhaps I may refer to that matter. The figures indicate that in my own province nearly 14 per cent of the work force is unemployed. This may not mean much to the Minister of Finance, who comes from Toronto and has relatively little concern or knowledge about what happens in other parts of the nation. Perhaps Ontario, with 8.6 per cent of its work force unemployed, seems rather insignificant to the minister. However, the figure is 13.9 per cent in British Columbia and it is higher in the maritimes. This is something that should concern the Minister of Finance more than it does.

We know there is conflict between the governor of the Bank of Canada and the Minister of Finance about what should be done, one taking a course of action that is in reality critical of the government in office and the other, namely the Minister of Finance, sitting idly by, engrossed in some book or other and not too much concerned about these matters.
We have listened to a very severe and biting indictment of the Minister of Finance and his government delivered by the hon. member who just resumed his seat, the hon. member for Assiniboia and others. These criticisms have been made not only today; they have been made on other occasions, both inside and outside the house. There have been complaints about the silly and childish way in which this government and this minister approach the question of our economy.
These are justifiable complaints when we have 700,000 of our potential working force sitting idly around, not knowing where their next dollar is coming from, while the Minister of Finance also sits idly around and obviously does not worry too much about it. "After all, spring came just the other day; there is no need to do anything about it," is the approach of this government. Perhaps the Minister of Finance should advise his colleague the Minister of Labour, to change the "Do It Now" slogan to "Why Wait For Summer; Do It Now".
In the minds of the minister and his colleagues this sort of thing might help, and this is the fullest extent to which this government is prepared to go. Their attitude is, "Let somebody else do it." So far as concrete and definite action to deal with the unemployment situation is concerned, this government has not the faintest idea what to do.
The Minister of Finance sits quietly in his seat asking the infrequent question and commenting occasionally. He sits here while all this controversy is raging as it has raged particularly today. I think that is only another indication of how lightly he takes his responsibility toward the unemployed of this nation.
I think the Minister of Finance should have been one of the first in the house to rise and announce specifically what is government policy in this field, or what is going to occur and how they are going to deal with the questions raised by the governor of the Bank of Canada in his annual report.
Are the government going to arrange, as they should, to open up these documents and the policies to the public eye? Are the government going to approach the question by allowing the annual report of the governor of the Bank of Canada to be made available for study by the banking and commerce
Interim. Supply
committee or some other special committee? Is this what is going to happen?
What is the approach of the government in so far as interest rates are concerned? What about the need, if it exists-and I think the need is very quickly approaching-for a new bond conversion program to get the minister out of the difficulty he got himself into a couple of years ago? These are serious and important matters. More than 700,000 people are tramping the streets in the middle of winter-even though spring is here according to the calendar it is not, in fact, here-not knowing whether government policies designed to assist them are going through. For the Minister of Finance to sit quietly in his place and decline to announce what is going to be done is an indication of the lightness with which he regards the economic difficulties of the nation. One of the things which I think must happen before we go much farther into the motion before us, is for the minister to rise and make some rather extensive announcements of policy and the like in connection with these matters which have been raised today and on other occasions.
We are not just using words and talking about statistics and pieces of paper and about whether or not they were supposed to be released this morning but were delivered inadvertently by a messenger to somebody else than the one intended. That is not what is at issue. The subject matter here is 719,000 people who are out of work because we have in office a bungling government without the vaguest idea of what to do and one which, even if it had such an idea, does not possess the courage to stand up and make announcements of its plans in the house.
It is a quarter to six by the clock. Perhaps what little the minister has to announce he might be able to announce in 15 minutes. It is possible his statement could be completed by that time. I think that is the only course open to the minister at the moment. Otherwise we are justified in arriving even more firmly at the conclusion that the hon. gentleman's interest in the unemployed is really not what he would have us believe.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Shall the resolution carry?

Before it carries, I think the Minister of Finance has a duty and responsibility which he cannot evade. I think it is up to him to stand up and make a statement about what the government intends to do in this particular field. I think that opportunity should be afforded him.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have the duty and the responsibility to tell some hon. members that, in speaking as they have spoken
