this afternoon in a manner which, I think, is virtually an abuse of the proper procedure on a motion for interim supply, they are creating a situation where we may not be able to get out the cheques for the mid-April payments, as we wish to do, because parliament has decided that we shall be rising next Wednesday and not returning until April 10.
A point of order-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is another bogus one.

The minister has no right to make a remark of that kind. He has now the opportunity of having this matter disposed of forthwith. Instead, he is making an imputation directed against all those who have taken part in this debate.
That is not a point of order.

It is a point of order, and I resent the imputation of the Minister of Finance that because we are discussing important public issues we are thereby open to the charge that we are preventing certain people in this country from receiving their remuneration.
That is exactly what you are doing.
It is not the case. This government could decide right now to relieve itself of its present parliamentary obligation. If there is any delay, it will be due to the intransigence of this government.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I should be obliged, Mr. Chairman, as I think would all members of this committee, if you would tell the hon. member for Essex East that he abuses the privileges of this house by raising bogus points of order. He offends against the rules at all times, and I think it is time he was rebuked by the Chair for so doing.
Having had my time taken by this bogus point of order, may I return to the point I was making. For years, with the exception only of these very recent years, these motions for interim supply passed very quickly. It was an extraordinary thing if there was any discussion on them at all. In recent times the opposition has chosen to debate, on this motion, any issue at all. This afternoon the Leader of the Opposition and one other hon. member talked about airing grievances. Mr. Chairman, they talked as though this were a motion to resolve the house into committee of supply. We are in committee of supply now, so that kind of procedure is clearly not the kind of procedure in which we are engaged at this time.
When the announcement was made that we would be asking for a vote of interim
[Mr. Fleming (Eglinton).l
supply this afternoon, I think all hon. members were well aware that the house had decided to rise next Wednesday and not to return until April 10 and that there is some other important business which must be transacted before we rise. There is to be dealt with the whole of those final supplementary estimates consisting of more than 100 items, and if hon. members choose on occasions of this kind to talk about every item under the sun and to raise all kinds of political issues for which there will be ample occasion in the ordinary course of parliamentary business for full discussion, it is inevitable that we shall not be able to get this vote of interim supply through before the time appointed to rise next Wednesday. I have to tell the committee that if this should happen there will be delay in getting out the cheques for the mid-April payments. The responsibility in that regard will have to rest with those who have taken advantage of this motion today and the ruling made by the Chair last year to bring into this discussion today about every kind of political issue under the sun.
I am not asking for a ruling from the Chair in view of the ruling which was made last year. I protested against this kind of procedure last year, but the Chair did not uphold the point I raised. I therefore cannot do anything about it, and if hon. members wish to bring in political issues and talk about everything under the sun I presume nothing can be done to stop them. But I do point out to them that there will be proper opportunity for the discussion of all these various matters which have been raised today. We have the estimates of all the departments before us to be considered in committee of supply with the exception of one department, the Department of Citizenship and Immigration whose estimates have been fully reviewed and passed. If we do not get this vote through I point out the inevitable results with respect to these mid-April cheques.
I would remind hon. members that this is a vote of interim supply and that I have given the time-honoured undertaking that nothing done here today by way of approving interim supply for two months will affect or abridge the rights of hon. members to discuss these items when they are reached in the ordinary course in committee. So everybody has his full rights. It is not necessary that hon. members should seize this opportunity to drag up all kinds of political issues. If that sort of thing happens we shall simply have to accept the fact that we cannot get these motions through. If there is to be no limit at all on the right of hon. members to discuss everything under the sun, we are in

a chaotic condition with regard to such motions as this. I appeal to the committee to have regard to the realities of the situation and to pass this simple motion knowing that the rights of members to discuss any question that is relevant to any item in committee are preserved.

I wonder if I could deal with one point which the minister has raised. I refer to the accusation that members in the opposition parties are responsible for delay. I would point out to the minister that it is the responsibility of the minister himself to decide if and when it is necessary to bring in an interim supply motion. It is his responsibility, and all he is doing now is admitting how delinquent this government is in its management of the bringing of motions before parliament. The minister knew a long time ago he would need interim supply. The fault is his entirely for deliberately forestalling this request until practically the eve of the Easter recess so he could make accusations of the kind in which he has indulged. The minister's own delinquency is responsible for this situation. The hon. gentleman is entirely incapable of operating properly.
The minister brought forward supplementary estimates that have to be dealt with. Do you realize, Mr. Chairman, that this is the fifth set of supplementary estimates we have had since the estimates a year ago? Five times he found out how wrong he was about his budget.
And five times the hon. member has made the same speech.

Listen to this, my hon. friend from Vancouver South. Perhaps the Minister of Finance should also listen and learn how he is participating in the breach of a contract between the government and parliament. I refer hon. members to the citation in Beau-chesne's in which reference is made to breach of contract between the government and parliament and which reads-

speechtext:
Order. We are not
discussing supplementary estimates at the moment but interim supply.

The minister raised the question of supplementary estimates and said it was necessary to deal with them before the Easter recess. I point out that he is guilty of a breach of contract between the government and parliament. This is the fifth time this has happened.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. We cannot have a debate on this subject.

The minister stood in his place and levelled accusations against us with
Interim Supply
respect to his inability to write cheques and so on. He has admitted his own delinquency and inability to be Minister of Finance but he cannot rid himself of the responsibilities that are associated with that office.
The hon. member has just rid himself of an insulting speech.
All the hon. member's speeches are insulting.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order.

I am dealing with the insulting remarks and accusations of the minister. He makes accusations of this insulting nature against the opposition. There are 700,000 people out of work. What is the minister's policy? I realize it is difficult for the government to face up to this question. The government levels insulting accusations. The minister's insults have to be answered in this fashion. I am not worried about the insulting accusations of the hon. member for Essex West or anyone else. I only know that 13.9 per cent of the working force in British Columbia from where I come are tramping the streets at the moment wondering when this minister will in the field of monetary policy take action to help them.
Instead of helping, the minister gave a five-minute lecture on how he wants the rules to operate so he can curtail business and conduct the affairs of parliament in his own way. I say that parliament should stand up to the minister and show Canadians how arrogant, delinquent, silly and childish is this hon. gentleman.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to confess that I also felt the Minister of Finance had evaded the chief issues raised here this afternoon. The hon. gentleman raised a bogey when he suggested that any discussion on parliamentary procedure at this time and of this type was unusual.
I wish to draw to the attention of the minister his assertions when in opposition. As recently as 1957 during his last term sitting on this side in opposition, the minister took up six pages of Hansard in speechmaking at this stage of our proceedings.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: On an occasioi when no undertaking was given, on the eve of an election.
Oh, oh.

I refer the hon. gentleman to page 2821 of Hansard of March 29,
1957.	The minister suggested that democracy might perhaps take a backward step because this parliament would not do its duty with respect to widows, orphans and civil servants. He suggested this would follow if we did

Interim Supply
not have an adequate parliamentary authorization. 1 refer the minister to his activities during the time when he was in opposition. The hon. gentleman did not say that to you, Mr. Chairman, earlier.
I also refer to the previous year, 1956, when in the same month we had a requirement for interim supply. I give the Conservative opposition of that day full credit. Hon. gentlemen at that time were not inactive nor did they in any way forsake their duties to the public. They properly took up debate at this stage. The record of that debate indicates that pages of Hansard were filled with speeches made by such well known hon. members as the present high commissioner in London, the former leader of the opposition, Mr. Drew. Speeches were also made by the present Minister of Trade and Commerce, the Postmaster General, the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources and other hon. gentlemen.
It is a well known and recognized privilege of hon. members of parliament, when a government asks for supply, to raise questions which they feel are proper in the interests of the Canadian public and no person has taken longer than has the Minister of Finance.

Hon. members opposite have had their inning by now. They know that these items will be called in the committee of supply in due course. Surely we can have this resolution passed now, Mr. Chairman. The bill must follow. It must be passed in the Senate and must receive royal assent. If it does not do so along with all the other business that must be presented before parliament rises at six o'clock next Wednesday for the Easter recess, then the cheques for the payment of salaries, pensions and other obligations for mid-April are going to be delayed.

Mr. Speaker, may I address a question to the house leader before inquiring about the business for tomorrow. Although last year we discussed interim supply about two days later than the date on which we are proceeding this year, would the leader of the house, in view of the remarks of the Minister of Finance concerning the importance of this matter, indicate whether or not it is proposed that an opportunity for debate on this question will be given early tomorrow? I ask because of course, some days will ensue before the end of the fiscal year.
